Calibrate a partially specified DAG to match target values

calibrate_dag.Rd

This function may be used to calibrate certain parameters in a partially specified DAG, given some global targets. For example, users may be interested in fixing marginal effects (such as the average causal treatment effect), rather than fixing the conditional treatment effects as represented by beta coefficients. See details.

Usage

calibrate_dag(lazy_dag, targets, params, n_sim_run=100000,
              n_sim_eval=1000000, n_reps_eval=1,
              seed=stats::runif(1, 0, 100),
              optimizer="auto", optim_method=NULL,
              optim_control=list(maxit=200), objective_fun=NULL,
              ...)

Arguments

lazy_dag

An unevaluated, partially specified lazy_DAG object created using the lazy_dag function. See ?lazy_dag for more information on lazy DAGs and the associated param() syntax. See ?node for general information on how to define DAGs.

targets

A list containing one list per desired target. These sub-lists need to contain at least two named elements: target, a numeric value specifying the exact desired value of the target and eval_fun, a function to evaluate the target value given simulated data with n_sim_run individuals or the current version of the DAG (if an additional use_dag=TRUE element is included). The eval_fun should only have one argument, which is the simulated data or DAG, and return exactly one numeric value relating to the target. Additionally, users may include a scale element, which should be a single numeric value specifying a scaling factor included during optimization. If not supplied, it defaults to 1. May be useful when targets are on widely different scales. This argument may specify any number of targets. See details, examples and the associated vignette.

params

A named list specifying the free parameters of the partially specified DAG. The names must correspond to the parameter placeholders introduced by param() in the lazy_dag. Each parameter specification must contain a finite numeric start value and may optionally contain the following elements:

range: A numeric vector of length two specifying the lower and upper bounds for the parameter. If omitted, the parameter is treated as unbounded. Bounds are used by optimization methods that support them. For a single parameter and a single target, a finite range is required for automatic root finding using uniroot.

scale: A positive numeric scalar specifying the parameter scale used by the numerical optimizer. If omitted, the scale is determined automatically from the parameter range or starting value.

Parameter specifications may be supplied as named lists or named numeric vectors when all supplied elements are scalar. For example, list(par1 = c(start = 1)) and list(par1 = list(start = 1)) are both valid. If the DAG contains only one free parameter, its specification may be supplied directly, without an additional named list, e.g. list(start = 0, range = c(-5, 5)). In this case, the parameter name is inferred from the corresponding param() placeholder.

n_sim_run

A single positive number, specifying the sample size that should be used when evaluating the targets during optimization. Higher numbers lead to more stable, reliable and precise estimates, but may take much longer to run. It often makes sense to use a smaller number first, to adjust the starting values with the (perhaps non-converged) results and to then re-run calibrate_dag() with a much higher value for more precise results.

n_sim_eval

A single positive number, specifying the sample size used when evaluating the targets after optimization has finished. This is primarily done to estimate how well the optimization worked. To obtain reliable and precise results, it should either be a fairly large number with a single simulation repetition (e.g. n_reps_eval=1), or a moderate number with a large number of repetitions. The latter has the advantage that sampling distributions can be plotted and confidence intervals can be estimated, but it comes at the cost of higher computation time.

n_reps_eval

A single positive number, specifying how many simulation repetitions should be performed when evaluating the final parameter values. See n_sim_eval.

seed

A random number generator seed. If not NULL, this seed is used on every single evaluation of the underlying changing DAG, eliminating some random sampling variation. The only exception is the final evaluation using a sample of size n_sim_eval, which instead uses seed + 1 (if possible), to make the evaluation independent of the optimization. Set to NULL to use an independent dataset during each optimization iteration instead.

optimizer

A single character string, specifying which optimizer should be used. Allowed values are: "uniroot" to use uniroot, "optim" to use optim, "optim2" to use the optim2 function from the calibrar package, "optimh" to use the optimh function from the calibrar package and "auto" (default), which is equal to "uniroot" whenever possible (e.g. whenever there is one target, one free parameter and defined bounds on that parameter) and equal to "optim" otherwise.

optim_method

A single character string, specifying which method should be used in the underlying optimizer function call. Ignored if "uniroot" is used as an optimizer.

optim_control

This argument is directly passed to the control argument of the respective optimiter function. Ignored if "uniroot" is used as an optimizer.

objective_fun

A custom function that should be used in the underlying optimizer function call to evaluate how close the current value of the targets are to the desired results. Any function that takes a numeric vector of (scaled) differences between the desired and estimated value and returns a scalar number that can be minimized may be used. Ignored if "uniroot" is used as an optimizer.

...

Further arguments passed to the optimizer and the sim_n_datasets function, which is used internally to generate one dataset (using n_repeats = 1). All named arguments are first passed through the optimizer.

Details

We recommend consulting the associated vignette for a more detailed explanation, including multiple worked examples, available at vignette(topic="v_calibrate_dag", package="simDAG").

What it does:

This function tries to help find suitable conditional parameters, when the goal is to fix marginal ones. Instead of defining all conditional parameters directly, users may specify arbitrary (potentially marginal) global parameters instead and to leave the conditional parameters partially unspecified. It then tries to calibrate the unspecified parameters, so that the global targets are met. The resulting DAG can then be used to simulate the data with the desired global target properties using sim_from_dag, sim_discrete_time or sim_discrete_event.

How it works:

Instead of defining a fully specified DAG, users should define only a partially specified DAG, leaving one or more parameters unspecified. This should be done using the lazy_dag function (see ?lazy_dag for more information). Afterwards, users can define an arbitrary amount of targets through custom targets functions. These functions should simply calculate the current value of the desired property. For example, if the data should have a 50% prevalence in the binary variable Y, a suitable target function would simply be function(data) {mean(data$Y)} with an associated target = 0.5. Additionally, users should give rough ranges in which the unspecified parameters may lie.

Internally, root finding (if 1 target and 1 unspecified parameter, with defined ranges) or numerical optimization (all other cases) is then used to find suitable values for the unspecified parameters that satisfy the target properties defined by the user. In a nutshell, the function simply simulates a large dataset from a given parameter combination, checks the resulting target properties and tries again. This idea, although applied in a less general setting, is also described by Austin and Stafford (2008) and Austin (2023).

To inspect the found parameter values and how well those produce the desired targets, users may use the associated summary() method (see examples). If n_reps_eval > 1, the associated plot.calibrated_DAG method may also be used. To simulate data directly using the resulting parameters, users may use the dag object returned in the output.

Currently supported features:

Users may use custom functions to define the target properties, so there are very few limits to what can be specified. Additionally, any parameter in a valid expression that defines a DAG may be left unspecified. Furthermore, there is no limit put on either the number of target properties (denoted \(m\)) or the number of unspecified parameters (denoted \(p\)), although some care needs to be exercised. If \(p > m\), there may be multiple different solutions, which is usually not problematic, but should be noted. If \(m > p\), there likely aren't any solutions, unless some targets are highly correlated. DAGs of any kind (using discrete-time varying covariates, continuous-time varying covariates, network dependencies, ...) may be used here.

Limitations:

There is unfortunately no guarantee that a solution for any given specification exist. Even worse, there is no guarantee that if a solution exists, that this function will find it. It is, however, still much better than manually searching for a solution. Furthermore, users should keep in mind that even if a solution exists and the numeric optimization is able to converge to it, that the results are only approximate. In most cases, this should be completely fine for Monte-Carlo simulation studies. However, in some edge cases, if exact simulation specifications of marginal parameters are required, this may not be sufficient.

Convergence:

Convergence may be tricky with complicated DAGs, many params or many targets (or both). Ultimately, the same techniques that work for any numerical optimization may be used to obtain convergence, e.g. tuning the optim_control arguments, re-running the function with starting values from a previous run etc. The only thing specific to this function that has a large effect on convergence is the n_sim_run argument. Better convergence may be obtained with larger values, at the price of a longer computation time.

Value

Returns a calibrated_DAG object. This object is basically just a list, containing the following objects:

  • inputs: A list containing all user inputs.

  • dag: A fully specified DAG, using the best sets of parameter values found to satisfy the user targets. This DAG may be directly used for simulation purposes.

  • est_params: The final parameter values after optimization.

  • target_eval: A final estimate of the targets, evaluated on the final DAG. If the function call was successful, these should be very close to the desired target parameters. If n_reps_eval > 1, these correspond to the average over all simulation repetitions.

  • d_target_eval: If n_reps_eval > 1 was used, this object includes three data.tables, including the estimated targets on each simulation run, the differences to the desired values and the scaled differences.

  • optim_obj: If optim, optim2 or optimh was used, the resulting object from that function call.

  • uniroot: If uniroot was used, the resulting object from that function call.

Robin Denz

Examples

library(simDAG)
library(data.table)
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘data.table’
#> The following object is masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     %notin%

# Example 1: Calibrate a single parameter to match a target prevalence.
# A finite parameter range allows automatic root finding.

ldag <- lazy_dag(
  empty_dag() +
    node("X", type="rnorm") +
    node("A", type="binomial", formula= ~ param(intercept_A) + X*0.5)
)

targets <- list(
  prevalence_A = list(
    target = 0.4,
    eval_fun = function(data) mean(data$A)
  )
)

# For a single parameter, its specification can be supplied directly.
params <- list(
  start = 0,
  range = c(-5, 5)
)

fit <- calibrate_dag(
  lazy_dag = ldag,
  targets = targets,
  params = params,
  n_sim_run = 2000,
  n_sim_eval = 5000,
  seed = 123
)
summary(fit)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Calibrated DAG
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Parameters (1)
#>    parameter estimate start lower upper parscale
#>  intercept_A  -0.3881     0    -5     5       NA
#> 
#> Targets (1)
#>        target desired achieved  error scaled_error
#>  prevalence_A     0.4   0.4186 0.0186       0.0186
#> 
#> Optimization
#>   Method:       uniroot
#>   Convergence:  successful
#>   Root residual: 0
#>   Iterations:   9
#>   Simulations:  2,000 optimization; 5,000 final evaluation
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# use final DAG to simulate data
data <- sim_from_dag(fit$dag, n_sim=10)
head(data)
#>              X      A
#>          <num> <lgcl>
#> 1: -0.39968354  FALSE
#> 2: -1.08779926   TRUE
#> 3: -1.09722672  FALSE
#> 4: -1.15883079   TRUE
#> 5: -0.03121757  FALSE
#> 6: -0.40738889   TRUE

# Example 2: Jointly calibrate treatment and outcome prevalence.
# The DAG contains two free parameters and two targets.
# Parameter ranges are optional.

ldag <- lazy_dag(
  empty_dag() +
    node("X", type="rnorm") +
    node("A", type="binomial",
         formula= ~ param(intercept_A) + X * 0.5) +
    node("Y", type="binomial",
         formula= ~ param(intercept_Y) + A * 0.7 + X * 0.4)
)

targets <- list(
  prevalence_A = list(
    target = 0.4,
    eval_fun = function(data) mean(data$A)
  ),
  prevalence_Y = list(
    target = 0.3,
    eval_fun = function(data) mean(data$Y)
  )
)

params <- list(
  intercept_A = list(start = 0),
  intercept_Y = list(start = 0)
)

fit <- calibrate_dag(
  lazy_dag = ldag,
  targets = targets,
  params = params,
  n_sim_run = 2000,
  n_sim_eval = 5000,
  seed = 123,
  optim_control = list(
    maxit = 200,
    trace = 0,
    ndeps = c(0.05, 0.05),
    factr = 100
  )
)
summary(fit)
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Calibrated DAG
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Parameters (2)
#>    parameter estimate start lower upper parscale
#>  intercept_A  -0.3828     0  -Inf   Inf        1
#>  intercept_Y  -1.1368     0  -Inf   Inf        1
#> 
#> Targets (2)
#>        target desired achieved  error scaled_error
#>  prevalence_A     0.4   0.4204 0.0204       0.0204
#>  prevalence_Y     0.3   0.3118 0.0118       0.0118
#> 
#> Optimization
#>   Optimizer:    optim()
#>   Method:       L-BFGS-B
#>   Convergence:  unsuccessful (code 52)
#>   Objective:    5e-07
#>   Evaluations:  function 47, gradient 47
#>   Message:      ERROR: ABNORMAL_TERMINATION_IN_LNSRCH
#>   Simulations:  2,000 optimization; 5,000 final evaluation
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# use final DAG to simulate data
data <- sim_from_dag(fit$dag, n_sim=10)
head(data)
#>             X      A      Y
#>         <num> <lgcl> <lgcl>
#> 1: -1.9845624  FALSE  FALSE
#> 2:  0.5216279   TRUE   TRUE
#> 3: -0.5202400  FALSE  FALSE
